To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
(1) the time spent stripping the cows is critical to the timeliness of all of the miliking chores, and (2) feeding time is determined primarily by how the feeding sys-tem is managed.

milking time is determined more strongly by how the milking system is managed than the type of milking system, and that feeding time is deter-mined more by how the feed system is managed than how the feed system operates.

the milking chore simulation results show that a milker using three units can machine-strip the cows in 10 s or less and still perform all milking chores in the allotted 20 min if the cows are prepped by a helper, and that feeding time is more dependent upon how the feeding system and the milking operation are managed than upon the type of feeding and milking system.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development of an integrated milking-feeding chore simulation model which will aid the dairy manager in evaluating and improving his milking and feeding systems.
the design of the milking and feeding systems and with the management of the milking, feeding and other chores in the barn.

the development of a computerized milking and feeding chore simulation model which can be used to evaluate the effect of various milking and feeding system design and management alternatives upon the time required to complete the milking and feeding tasks in a timely manner, and to determine the effects of various milking machine stripping time requirements upon the timeliness and efficiency of the milking and other chores.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the milking and feeding systems used in confinement-stall barn operations should be carefully planned and managed to ensure that the chores are completed in a timely manner.
the type of system used is of secondary importance compared with the management of the system.
the milking and feeding systems must be managed to ensure that all of the chores are done in a timely fashion.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the milking chore simulation results indicate that milker performance is the limiting factor in the milking operation and that feeding time is not a limiting factor in the feeding operation.
milking and feeding systems must be designed to minimize the time spent in the barn.
the milker's time is not wasted in the feeding chores, but rather is spent on the milking chores, which is where the time is needed.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the milking chore is not a simple, linear process.

it is possible to develop a simulation model that can be used to evaluate the impact of milking chore time on the timeliness of other chores, and that the model could be used to evaluate milking and feeding chore time for various types of systems and management practices.
the milker is a key component to a well-functioning milking and feeding operation.
